theme: The law as guardian; sons not slaves; Hagar and Sarah
readingInstruction: Read Galatians 3:1-4:31. This long reading is Paul’s theological argument. Notice his use of Abraham and the promise, the purpose of the law, and the allegory of Hagar and Sarah. Pay special attention to 3:23-29.
settingTheScene: Paul has shown in chapters 1 and 2 that the gospel does not come from men, and that justification is not by works of the law. Now he turns to argue from Scripture and experience. He appeals first to the Galatians’ own experience of receiving the Spirit, then to Abraham, then to the purpose of the law. He answers a question the false teachers raised: if the law doesn’t justify, why was it given?
observation: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?” (3:1).
“Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for The righteous shall live by faith” (3:11).
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (3:13).
“So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith” (3:24).
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (3:28).
“And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (3:29).
“My little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you” (4:19).
“Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise” (4:28).
interpretation:
Paul begins with a rebuke and a question: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.” Then he asks: “Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?” They received the Spirit when they first believed, by faith, not by works. Why think they will be perfected by the flesh?

Next Abraham: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” So the sons of Abraham are those of faith. Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith and preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham: “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” Those who rely on works of the law are under a curse, for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.” No one does. But “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.” The cross is where the curse fell. This was so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, and we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.

The law came 430 years after the promise and cannot annul it. If the inheritance comes by law, it no longer comes by promise, but God gave it to Abraham by promise. “Why then the law?” It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come. It was a temporary measure. It does not contradict the promises, but it could not give life. “So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.” The guardian (Greek paidagogos) was a slave who supervised a child, not a teacher. His job ended when the child grew up. This is a key text for understanding the relationship between the covenants: the Mosaic covenant had a temporary role in God’s plan, and Christ has brought its fulfillment. Christians differ over how much of the law continues to apply as moral guidance; all agree that it is not a means of justification, and that Christ fulfills it.

Then comes one of the greatest statements about the church: “For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.” All the divisions that separated people are overcome. Every believer has the same standing and the same inheritance. This does not erase all distinctions, but it removes them as grounds for status before God.

Chapter 4 continues with adoption (see yesterday’s pause) and Paul’s pastoral heart: “My little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you.” Then the allegory of Hagar and Sarah. Hagar represents the covenant from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery, corresponding to the present Jerusalem. Sarah represents the free woman, the Jerusalem above. “Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.” The one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born by the Spirit, and so it is now. But “what does the Scripture say? Cast out the slave woman and her son.” We are not children of the slave but of the free woman.
connection: Genesis 12:1-3, 15:1-6, and 17 are the Abrahamic covenant. Exodus 19 to 20 is Sinai. Deuteronomy 27:26 and 21:23 are cited in 3:10 and 3:13. Habakkuk 2:4 is cited in 3:11. Genesis 16 and 21 tell of Hagar and Sarah. Isaiah 54:1 is cited in 4:27. Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises the new covenant. Romans 4 gives a parallel argument. Hebrews 8 to 10 explain the old and new covenants. Colossians 2:16-17 says the old is a shadow and the substance belongs to Christ. Revelation 21:2 speaks of the new Jerusalem.
application:
Ask where you are trying to be perfected by the flesh after beginning in the Spirit.

Thank Christ for becoming a curse for you. Say it slowly.

Seek out someone different from you, in age, background, or status, and show them the unity we have in Christ.
prayerPrompts: Thank Christ for becoming a curse for you.
Thank him that you are a son or daughter and not a slave.
Ask him to teach you to live in that freedom.
